query: Consider the following context: High entropy alloys have excellent wear resistance, so they have great application prospects in the fields of wear resistance and surface protection. In that context, which material can be used for adhere to the surface of a Cu matrix, and why?

generation.hypothesis: In a Cu-based composite, a graded Ni‐based interlayer applied prior to the deposition of a high-entropy alloy (HEA) coating improves the adhesion and durability of the composite under wear and thermal cycling conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: A polished copper (Cu) substrate with its native oxide layer possibly present.
generation.intervention: Apply a thin, graded Ni‐based interlayer using controlled deposition and substrate heating, followed by deposition of a refractory HEA coating.
generation.conditions: Subject the coated Cu substrate to cyclic thermal loading and frictional wear typical of service environments where both electrical/thermal conductivity and high wear resistance are required.
generation.structural_mediator: The Ni-based interlayer mediates interdiffusion bonding at the Cu/HEA interface and reduces thermal expansion mismatches by gradually transitioning from Cu to the HEA composition.
generation.mechanism: The graded Ni‐based interlayer promotes metallurgical bonding via diffusion at the interface, thereby reducing stress concentrations caused by thermal expansion differences. This leads to improved adhesion and resistance to delamination when the composite is exposed to wear and thermal cycling.
generation.predicted_outcome: The composite with the Ni‐based interlayer will exhibit higher adhesion strength, lower wear rates, and improved interfacial stability compared to systems with direct HEA deposition on Cu.
generation.baseline: Cu substrate with direct HEA coating deposition (lacking the graded interlayer), which is expected to have inferior adhesion due to poor metallurgical bonding and mismatched thermal properties.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies under conditions where the interfacial bonding is the primary challenge. Limitations may arise if extreme thermal mismatches or environmental corrosion factors dominate the failure mechanism beyond adhesion issues.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal thickness and composition profile of the Ni‐based interlayer need further experimental validation, and its long-term stability under severe cyclic thermal stresses requires additional investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set with a directly deposited HEA coating on Cu and a second set with a graded Ni‐based interlayer followed by the HEA coating. Subject both sample sets to identical cyclic thermal and wear testing regimes.
measurements: Adhesion strength via scratch tests and pull-off tests
Wear rate assessments under controlled tribological conditions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples with the Ni‐based interlayer do not demonstrate a statistically significant improvement in adhesion strength, wear resistance, and thermal cycling durability compared to the direct deposition samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High-entropy alloys (HEAs), since their discovery by Yeh et al. in 2004, [1] have opened up researchers to a new alloy system that contains five or more equimolar principal elements. In equimolar HEAs, each element has an equal probability of occupying the lattice sites in a crystal structure such as face-centered cubic (FCC), [2] body-centered cubic (BCC), [3] or hexagonal structure [4] crystal structures. Lattice distortion, sluggish diffusion, high entropy, and cocktail effects have been identified as the core effects contributing to the superior properties, hardness, strength, ductility, erosion, tribocorrosion, corrosion, and oxidation/wear resistance [5] − [7] of HEAs in a wide range of temperatures over conventional alloys. From the viewpoint of applications in extrusion dies and cutting inserts, the cost of metal powders used to develop bulk HEAs can hinder their commercialization as an alternative to the alloys in use. occupying_moves.lever: high entropy alloy composition and deposition parameters
occupying_moves.technique: physical vapor deposition (sputtering) combined with interface pre-treatment
occupying_moves.conditions: Deposition on a Cu substrate at controlled temperatures to enable interfacial diffusion bonding and enhanced adhesion

chosen.lever: optimized high entropy alloy composition tailored for interfacial reactivity
chosen.technique: sputtering deposition with pre-treated Cu surfaces
chosen.conditions: Room temperature to moderately elevated temperatures ensuring sufficient atomic intermixing while preserving the Cu matrix's integrity
chosen.why: This move directly addresses the open question by experimentally investigating which high entropy alloy composition adheres effectively to a Cu matrix. By controlling deposition parameters and interfacial chemistry, it fills the gap in previous studies that have not focused on interface bonding properties between high entropy alloy coatings and copper substrates.

frame.system: A composite or coated system where a high entropy alloy (HEA) is applied on a copper (Cu) matrix. The Cu substrate provides its intrinsic electrical/thermal properties while the HEA layer is expected to deliver excellent wear resistance.
frame.goal: To improve the surface wear resistance and protection of the Cu matrix by depositing a coating that not only has high hardness but also forms a strong metallurgical bond with the Cu substrate.
frame.limitation: Identifying a coating material that can be reliably adhered to the Cu matrix without issues such as poor bonding, thermal expansion mismatch, or phase incompatibility.
root_cause_cues: adhere to the surface of a Cu matrix
constraints: The material must be compatible with the Cu substrate to ensure adequate adhesion.
It should maintain the advantageous properties of both the Cu matrix (like conductivity) and the HEA (wear resistance).
Thermal and mechanical property matching is essential to avoid delamination or cracking under service conditions.
frame.regime: Typical conditions involving high wear or friction where surface degradation is a critical concern, potentially accompanied by thermal cycling due to frictional heating.
prior_attempts: Conventional wear-resistant coatings (e.g., carbides or nitrides) have been applied to Cu surfaces but often failed to provide a robust metallurgical bond because of significant differences in coefficient of thermal expansion or chemical incompatibility.
Simple deposition techniques may have resulted in weak interfacial bonding and poor long-term durability under cyclic loads.
frame.understanding: There is a need to design a coating system that not only provides the wear resistance typical of high entropy alloys but also overcomes the adhesion and compatibility issues when interfaced with a Cu matrix. Specifically, understanding the interfacial reactions, diffusion phenomena, and matching of thermophysical properties is critical in choosing the right alloy composition or introducing an interlayer (e.g., a Ni-based transition layer) to promote bonding.

decision.trend: Early studies on high entropy alloys largely focused on enhancing internal properties—mechanical strength, wear resistance, and microstructural refinement—using techniques like ball milling, spark plasma sintering, selective laser melting, and physical vapor deposition. More recent work (as in PMC7304825) has begun to address the challenges of thin film deposition where adhesion and interfacial integrity are critical, using methods such as DC-magnetron sputtering with subsequent annealing to improve film adhesion. However, almost all of these studies have concentrated on substrates like stainless steel or silicon, and the unique challenges when depositing on a Cu matrix (especially due to differences in thermal expansion and chemical compatibility) have not yet been directly solved.
decision.unsolved: The unresolved issue is how to reliably bond a high entropy alloy coating to a copper substrate so that the coating can impart its excellent wear resistance without succumbing to interfacial delamination or phase incompatibility. In other words, ensuring strong metallurgical bonding of an HEA on Cu remains a design challenge, particularly under conditions involving thermal cycling and frictional heating.
decision.lever: Implementing an interface pre‐treatment combined with optimized deposition parameters—specifically, using a controlled substrate heating protocol along with a thin, graded Ni‐based interlayer to mediate diffusion bonding between Cu and the HEA coating.
decision.why: This approach follows the trend of refining deposition and post-treatment techniques to improve interfacial adhesion in HEA films, as seen in recent works. The use of a graded interlayer (occupying the identified niche for interface modification) leverages both diffusion bonding and thermal expansion matching to resolve the adhesion issue on the Cu substrate while preserving the wear-resistance benefits of the HEA.
